title: Indexes
scopeHtml: Scope: B+tree internals, composite order, selectivity, covering and index-only scans, maintenance and incidents.

notes.title: Why indexes exist
notes.html:
An index is a separate, sorted structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table. Without one, WHERE email = 'a@x.com' must read every row (a sequential scan). With one, it jumps straight to the match, like the index at the back of a book.

Cost: every index uses disk and RAM, and slows every INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column and DELETE, because the index must be updated too. So you index for the queries you actually run.

Worked example (illustrative numbers). users has 10M rows, 1.2 GB. Seq scan at ~1 GB/s from cache is ~1 s; from cold disk much more. A B+tree lookup touches about 4 pages (root, two inner, leaf) plus 1 heap page: under 1 ms when cached. That is roughly a 1000x gain for a point lookup.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';
-- Before index:
--  Seq Scan on users  (cost=0.00..208334.00 rows=1 width=120) (actual time=412.3..412.3 rows=1 loops=1)
--    Filter: (email = 'a@x.com'::text)
--    Rows Removed by Filter: 9999999
--  Execution Time: 412.5 ms
CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);
-- After:
--  Index Scan using users_email_idx on users  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=120) (actual time=0.03..0.03 rows=1 loops=1)
--    Index Cond: (email = 'a@x.com'::text)
--  Execution Time: 0.05 ms

Industry examples. Every OLTP system lives and dies by its indexes; GitHub and Shopify engineering posts repeatedly trace outages to a missing or dropped index after a migration. Instagram's early Postgres tuning was largely index and partial-index work.

Everyday analogy. The index in a textbook: you look up "photosynthesis", get page numbers, and skip reading 600 pages.

Common interview traps.

  • "Add an index" with no thought for write cost.
  • Indexing every column. Each index slows writes and uses RAM.
  • Not mentioning that small tables are faster to scan than to index-seek.

notes.title: The B+tree: how the common index works
notes.html:
A B+tree is a balanced, wide, shallow tree whose leaf pages hold the sorted keys and are linked together. Both Postgres btree and MySQL InnoDB use it as the default.

Properties:

  • Wide nodes: one node is one disk page (Postgres 8 KB, InnoDB 16 KB), holding hundreds of keys. Fan-out of ~300 means 3 levels cover 300^3 = 27M keys and 4 levels cover ~8 billion. So even huge tables need 3 to 5 page reads.
  • Sorted leaves, linked left and right: range queries (BETWEEN, ORDER BY) find the start and walk sideways.
  • Inner nodes hold only separators (guideposts); real entries live in leaves.
  • Page splits: when a leaf is full, it splits into two and pushes a key up. Random inserts split often; sequential inserts append at the right edge cheaply.
                 [ 40 | 80 ]                  root (inner)
               /      |      \
      [10|20|30]  [50|60|70]  [90|100|110]    leaves (sorted, linked ->)
      (ptr to rows)    ->          ->
Lookup 60: root -> middle child -> leaf scan -> row pointer

What a leaf points to. InnoDB: the primary key B+tree IS the table (clustered); secondary index leaves store the PK value, so a secondary lookup is two tree descents (index, then PK tree). Postgres: leaves store a TID (page number plus slot) pointing into the heap, one jump.

Worked example. 100M rows, 8-byte key plus 6-byte TID plus overhead ~ 20 B/entry: 100M x 20 B = 2 GB leaf level, about 270k pages of 8 KB at ~90% full (default fillfactor 90 for B-tree indexes). Depth: 4 levels. Upper levels (a few thousand pages, ~20 MB) stay permanently in cache, so the real cost is roughly one leaf read plus one heap read.

Other index types (Postgres). Hash (equality only), GIN (arrays, jsonb, full text), GiST (geometry, ranges), SP-GiST, BRIN (tiny; for huge naturally ordered columns like timestamps in append-only tables). MySQL InnoDB: B+tree, plus full-text and spatial.

Decision gravity. Creating an index is reversible; the engineering risk is the build lock. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres (no write block, slower, can leave an INVALID index if it fails). MySQL 8 InnoDB builds most indexes online.

Everyday analogy. A library with a floor map: building -> floor -> shelf. Three signs get you to any book among millions.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying a B-tree and a B+tree are the same (data only in leaves for B+tree; leaves linked).
  • Thinking depth grows with row count linearly. It grows logarithmically with a huge base.
  • Using a B-tree for LIKE '%foo' (leading wildcard can't use it).

notes.title: Composite indexes and column order
notes.html:
A composite index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b within each a, then c within each (a, b). It works like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name.

The leftmost prefix rule: the index can serve queries that constrain a, or a, b, or a, b, c from the left. It can't efficiently serve a query on only b.

CREATE INDEX orders_cust_status_created ON orders (customer_id, status, created);
-- Uses index fully:   WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'paid' AND created > '2025-01-01'
-- Uses index prefix:  WHERE customer_id = 7
-- Cannot seek:        WHERE status = 'paid'            (no leading column)
-- Sorted output free: WHERE customer_id=7 AND status='paid' ORDER BY created

Ordering guideline (ESR style). Put equality columns first, then the sort column, then range columns last. A range condition on a column stops later columns from being used for seeking. With (customer_id, created, status), query customer_id = 7 AND created > X AND status = 'paid' can seek on the first two, but status becomes a filter inside the scanned range.

Worked example. orders has 50M rows, 500k customers (100 rows each), 5 statuses. Query customer_id = 7 AND status = 'paid'. Index (customer_id, status) reads ~20 rows. Index (status, customer_id) also works for this query, but is less reusable: WHERE customer_id = 7 alone can't seek it. Reverse the question: pick the order that serves the most query shapes, high-selectivity equality columns first.

ORDER BY and direction. An index can be read backwards, so (a ASC, b ASC) serves ORDER BY a DESC, b DESC; mixed directions (a ASC, b DESC) need an index declared that way (CREATE INDEX ON t (a ASC, b DESC)).

Do not duplicate. (a, b) makes a separate (a) index redundant (only exception: a much smaller (a) index for scan speed). Audit with pg_stat_user_indexes (idx_scan = 0 over weeks means unused).

MySQL note. MySQL 8 can do index skip scan in limited cases, and loose index scan for some group-by queries; do not rely on it. Postgres 18 adds skip-scan for B-tree (confirm version notes) but design as if the prefix rule holds.

Everyday analogy. A phone book by (last name, first name). You can find all "Sharma"; you can't find all "Rahul" without reading the whole book.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting the range column before equality columns.
  • Creating (a) and (a, b) and (a, b, c) together.
  • Believing column order does not matter.

notes.title: Selectivity and when the planner ignores your index
notes.html:
Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition keeps; high selectivity means it keeps very few. email = X keeps 1 in 10M (great for an index). is_active = true keeping 95% is poor.

The planner estimates row counts from statistics (file 05) and chooses an index scan only when it expects it to be cheaper than a sequential scan. Index scans do random heap reads (expensive); seq scans read sequentially (cheap per page). Rule of thumb: once a filter returns more than roughly 5 to 15% of the table, a seq scan often wins. random_page_cost (default 4.0; ~1.1 on SSD) shifts that threshold.

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';
-- 90% of rows are paid:
--  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..105000.00 rows=9000000 width=40)
--    Filter: (status = 'paid'::text)
-- Planner correctly ignores an index on status.

Partial indexes fix skew. Index only the rare interesting rows:

CREATE INDEX orders_pending_idx ON orders (created) WHERE status = 'pending';
-- 0.1% of rows: tiny index, fast, cheap to maintain
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created LIMIT 50;

Cardinality order. Of a composite's equality columns, there is no absolute rule that the more selective goes first; design for query reuse. Still, an index on a low-cardinality column alone (boolean, gender, status) is usually useless.

Reasons an index is skipped even when you expect it.

  • Function on the column: WHERE lower(email) = 'a@x.com' needs an expression index ON users (lower(email)).
  • Type mismatch / implicit cast: comparing varchar column with a numeric parameter, or a MySQL string column compared to an integer (casts every row).
  • Leading wildcard: LIKE '%abc'. Use pg_trgm + GIN, or full text search.
  • OR across different columns; stale statistics; tiny table.
  • Non-deterministic arithmetic: WHERE created + interval '1 day' > now() (move the math to the constant side).

Industry examples. The "boolean flag index" and "function on column" are the two most common bugs found in slow-query reviews at product companies; Postgres partial indexes are a signature fix for queue-like tables (WHERE processed = false).

Everyday analogy. If almost every book is "fiction", the "fiction" index entry just says "go read the whole library", so you skip it and read straight through.

Common interview traps.

  • Indexing a boolean column and expecting speed.
  • Wrapping an indexed column in a function.
  • Not knowing partial indexes exist.

notes.title: Covering indexes and index-only scans
notes.html:
A covering index contains every column the query needs, so the database never visits the table. In Postgres this is an index-only scan; in MySQL it is "Using index" in EXPLAIN.

-- Query needs customer_id (filter) and total (output)
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_inc ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total);   -- Postgres 11+
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
--  Index Only Scan using orders_cust_inc on orders (cost=0.56..4.60 rows=20 width=4)
--                                  (actual time=0.02..0.03 rows=20 loops=1)
--    Index Cond: (customer_id = 7)
--    Heap Fetches: 0
--    Buffers: shared hit=4

INCLUDE columns are stored in leaf pages only, not used for ordering or uniqueness; good for adding payload without widening the search key. MySQL has no INCLUDE; add the columns to the key, but secondary indexes automatically include the PK columns.

Postgres visibility catch. Postgres can only skip the heap for a page if the visibility map says all rows on it are visible to everyone. After heavy updates, Heap Fetches is large and the "index-only" scan still reads the heap. VACUUM (autovacuum) sets the map bits. A write-heavy table can show an Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches near the row count.

Worked example. Dashboard query returns 20 rows per request at 5,000 requests/s. Plain index scan: 20 index entries plus up to 20 heap pages = ~21 page touches; covering: ~4 pages. At 5,000 req/s, you save ~85k page touches per second, often the difference between 30% and 80% CPU. Cost: the index is bigger and updates of total now update the index too (no HOT update, see below).

HOT updates. Postgres can do a "heap-only tuple" update, skipping index maintenance, only if no indexed column changes and the page has room. Indexing a frequently updated column (like updated_at or a counter) kills HOT and bloats indexes.

InnoDB clustered detail. Because secondary indexes store the PK, a secondary index on (a) already covers queries needing (a, pk). A wide PK (a UUID string) bloats every secondary index.

Decision gravity. Covering indexes are a tuning trade you can undo cheaply (drop the index) but each is permanent write overhead; add them for the top few hot queries only.

Everyday analogy. A menu that lists the price beside each dish, so you never have to ask the kitchen.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming an Index Only Scan never touches the heap in Postgres (check Heap Fetches).
  • Adding INCLUDE columns that update constantly.
  • Using SELECT * and killing the possibility of an index-only plan.

notes.title: Index maintenance, bloat and production incidents
notes.html:
Indexes decay. Postgres MVCC leaves dead entries; autovacuum cleans them, but heavy churn causes bloat: an index 3x bigger than needed, more cache misses and slower scans. Rebuild without long locks: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+). MySQL: OPTIMIZE TABLE or ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=InnoDB (online DDL).

Useful checks:

-- Unused indexes (reset-aware: look at weeks of data)
SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid))
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan ASC LIMIT 10;
-- Invalid indexes left by a failed CONCURRENTLY build
SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

Incident 1: missing index after deploy. A new query filters by tenant_id, status. CPU climbs from 20% to 95% over an hour; pg_stat_statements shows the query with high total_exec_time; EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan ... Rows Removed by Filter: 40M. Fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

Incident 2: index build locks writes. Plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock; inserts and updates queue for 8 minutes on a 200 GB table; connection pool fills and the API 500s. Always CONCURRENTLY on live tables.

Incident 3: write amplification. A table with 14 indexes sustains 2k inserts/s instead of 15k, because each insert updates 14 B-trees and WAL grows 10x. Metric: WAL bytes/s and idx_tup_insert. Fix: drop unused and overlapping indexes.

Incident 4: random UUID PK. Insert latency rises as the table outgrows RAM (random leaf pages). Fix: time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, ULID, bigint).

Industry examples. GitHub's gh-ost and Percona's pt-online-schema-change exist because adding indexes on huge MySQL tables used to block; MySQL 5.6+ online DDL reduced but did not remove the need. Postgres shops use pg_repack for table and index bloat.

Decision gravity. Dropping an index is instant but the rebuild may take hours; before dropping an apparently unused one, check for rarely run jobs (month-end reports) and replicas (stats are per node).

Everyday analogy. A filing cabinet that gets messy with torn labels. You periodically re-sort it, ideally while the office is still open.

Common interview traps.

  • Running CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a hot table.
  • Dropping an "unused" index only checked on the primary, while reads happen on replicas.
  • Adding indexes as the answer to everything.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An index trades write cost and space for fast reads; add them for measured queries.
  • B+tree: wide shallow pages, sorted linked leaves; 3 to 5 page reads reach one row among billions.
  • InnoDB clustered PK vs Postgres heap with TID pointers changes secondary-index cost and PK choice.
  • Composite index: leftmost prefix; equality columns first, then sort, then range.
  • Low-selectivity filters get seq scans; fix skew with partial indexes; avoid functions/casts on indexed columns (or use expression indexes).
  • Covering indexes (INCLUDE) allow index-only scans; check Heap Fetches and vacuum health.
  • Build with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; prune unused and duplicate indexes; watch bloat and write amplification.

questions.subtopic: What an index buys and costs
questions.promptHtml: What does an index actually do, and why not just index every column?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see indexes as a read/write trade, not a free speed-up.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An index is a separate sorted structure that maps column values to row locations, so a lookup reads a handful of pages instead of the whole table. The price is paid on every write: each INSERT, DELETE and any UPDATE of an indexed column must also update every index, and each index takes disk and cache. So I index for queries I have measured, not for every column.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without an index, WHERE email = ? is a sequential scan: read every page, test every row. With a B+tree the database descends about 3 to 5 pages and then fetches the heap row, so a point lookup drops from hundreds of ms to well under 1 ms on a 10M-row table (illustrative).

The costs:

  • Writes: one extra B+tree insert per index. A table with 10 indexes does 11 structure updates per insert, and each is also WAL-logged.
  • Space and RAM: indexes compete with table pages for shared buffers and OS cache.
  • Planner and maintenance: more candidate plans, more bloat, longer VACUUM, slower DDL.
  • Small tables: scanning 50 pages is cheaper than an index seek plus random heap read, so the planner ignores the index anyway.
write path:  INSERT row -> heap page
                        -> index 1 leaf
                        -> index 2 leaf
                        -> ...  (each also WAL-logged)
read path:   WHERE email=? -> root -> inner -> leaf -> heap row

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_idx ON users (email);
-- illustrative plan after: Index Scan using users_email_idx ... (actual time=0.03..0.03 rows=1)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Indexing every column "just in case".
  • Forgetting that boolean or low-cardinality columns alone give the planner no reason to use the index.
  • Adding an index without checking that a real query uses it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which operations get slower with more indexes? -> INSERT, DELETE, and UPDATEs that touch an indexed column; also VACUUM and replication volume.
  2. When is a seq scan better than an index? -> Tiny tables, or when the filter keeps more than roughly 5 to 15% of rows.
  3. How do you find indexes that should not exist? -> pg_stat_user_indexes with idx_scan = 0 over weeks, checked on every replica, plus overlapping prefixes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "index makes reads fast, slows writes". The senior quantifies it (pages touched, write amplification, WAL volume), ties indexes to measured queries and names the audit process for removing them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routinely discover a table with a dozen indexes where half have zero scans, and insert throughput recovers after dropping them.

questions.promptHtml: How does a B+tree index work, and why can it find one row among a billion in a few page reads?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand fan-out and page-sized nodes rather than "it is a binary tree".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A B+tree is a wide, balanced tree where each node is one disk page holding hundreds of keys. With fan-out around 300, three levels cover about 27 million keys and four cover billions. Inner nodes only hold separators; the real entries sit in sorted, linked leaf pages, so a lookup is a few page reads and a range scan walks leaves sideways.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Node = page (Postgres 8 KB, InnoDB 16 KB). A page of 8 KB with ~20 byte entries holds a few hundred. Depth is log base ~300 of N, so it barely grows: 100M rows is about 4 levels.

              [ 40 | 80 ]                  root
            /     |      \
   [10|20|30] [50|60|70] [90|100|110]      leaves, linked ->
Lookup 60: root -> middle child -> leaf -> TID/PK -> heap row
  • Inner nodes: separators only. Leaves: key plus pointer (Postgres: TID of heap tuple; InnoDB secondary: the primary key value).
  • Leaves are linked, so BETWEEN and ORDER BY find the start and walk sideways.
  • Page split: when a leaf is full it splits and pushes a key up. Random inserts split often; ascending keys append at the right edge.
  • Top levels are a few thousand pages (~tens of MB), so they stay cached; real I/O is about one leaf plus one heap read.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling B-tree and B+tree identical. In a B+tree data pointers live only in leaves and leaves are linked.
  • Believing depth grows linearly with rows.
  • Expecting LIKE '%foo' to use it; the sort order cannot help a leading wildcard.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not a binary tree? -> One compare per page read is far too many I/Os; wide nodes make each I/O eliminate ~99.7% of candidates.
  2. What happens on a page split? -> Leaf divides in two, a separator is pushed to the parent, possibly cascading to the root which then grows the tree by one level.
  3. Hash index vs B+tree? -> Hash is equality only, no ordering or range; Postgres B-tree is the default because it serves equality, range and ORDER BY.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "balanced tree, O(log n)". Senior: page-sized nodes, fan-out arithmetic, cached upper levels, split behaviour with random vs sequential keys, and what a leaf points at in each engine.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Random UUID primary keys cause scattered leaf splits and cache misses once the index outgrows RAM.

questions.contextHtml:
A login endpoint does SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE lower(email) = lower($1). users has 8M rows and an index users_email_idx ON users (email). The endpoint takes ~350 ms and CPU on the primary is climbing. A teammate says "the index is there, so it must be the network".

-- illustrative
Seq Scan on users  (cost=0.00..201000.00 rows=40000 width=72) (actual time=0.1..340.2 rows=1 loops=1)
  Filter: (lower(email) = 'a@x.com'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 7999999
questions.promptHtml: Why is the index not used, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run ANALYZE" or "add another index on lower(email)" without explaining why the first one is useless, or "force an index scan with a hint". It misses that the predicate is on an expression, not the column.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is email stored with mixed case? (decides whether I can just normalise on write). How many writers? Is the column UNIQUE today?
  2. Immediate mitigation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_lower_idx ON users (lower(email)); Online, no write block.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) expression on the column defeats a plain B-tree; (b) stale stats; (c) implicit cast. The plan's Filter: (lower(email) = ...) and Rows Removed by Filter: 7999999 point at (a).
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) after the new index; expect Index Scan using users_email_lower_idx.
  5. Root cause: The B-tree is sorted by email, not lower(email); the planner cannot use that order to find lower-case matches, so it evaluates the function on every row.
  6. Fix: Short term: the expression index. Long term: citext column or normalise to lowercase on write with UNIQUE (email), so the query is a plain equality.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: no function on an indexed column in WHERE without a matching expression index; run pg_stat_statements for top total time after each release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop the old index blindly (other queries may use it) and would not disable seqscan globally.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the query is lower(email) LIKE 'a%'? -> Needs text_pattern_ops on the expression index unless the DB collation is C.
  • What if the plan still seq scans? -> Run ANALYZE users (expression indexes get their own stats) and check the query uses exactly the same expression.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration swapped a column to varchar and the ORM began casting parameters as numeric; every lookup became a seq scan and the primary hit 95% CPU within the hour. The fix was one line in the query layer and a note in the review checklist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network or "adds hardware".
  • Hire: identifies the function-on-column problem and proposes an expression index.
  • Strong hire: also fixes at the data-model level, uses CONCURRENTLY, and names the cast/collation variants.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the leftmost-prefix rule and how you decide column order in a composite index.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Column order is the most common index design mistake; it shows whether you reason from query shapes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A composite index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b within a, then c within (a, b). It can seek only on a leftmost prefix. My rule: equality columns first, then the ORDER BY column, then range columns last, because a range on a column stops later columns from narrowing the scan. Among equals I pick the order that serves the most query shapes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of a phone book by (last, first). You can find all "Sharma" or "Sharma, Rahul" but not all "Rahul".

CREATE INDEX orders_cust_status_created ON orders (customer_id, status, created);
-- seek on all three:  WHERE customer_id=7 AND status='paid' AND created > X
-- seek on prefix:     WHERE customer_id=7
-- cannot seek:        WHERE status='paid'
-- no sort needed:     WHERE customer_id=7 AND status='paid' ORDER BY created
  • With (customer_id, created, status) and customer_id=7 AND created > X AND status='paid', the scan seeks on the first two and status is only a filter inside the range.
  • Directions: an index can be read backwards, so (a, b) serves ORDER BY a DESC, b DESC; mixed directions need the index declared that way.
  • (a, b) makes a separate (a) redundant, apart from a smaller index for scan speed.
  • Postgres 18 adds B-tree skip scan (verify the release notes); design as if the prefix rule holds.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Range column before equality columns.
  • Creating (a), (a,b), (a,b,c) all together.
  • Choosing order only by "most selective first" and ignoring reuse across queries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't (a,b) serve WHERE b=? efficiently? -> Entries for a given b are scattered across every a, so there is no contiguous range to seek.
  2. Equality on a, ORDER BY c, filter on b: best index? -> (a, c) or (a, c, b)? Putting c before b gives sorted output and stops early with LIMIT; b becomes an index filter.
  3. When does mixed ASC/DESC matter? -> ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC cannot be read from an all-ASC index in either direction.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "leftmost prefix". Senior: ESR ordering, sort elimination with LIMIT, redundancy auditing and the cost of a range predicate on seek depth.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An index on (status, customer_id) served the dashboard but not the customer page, leading to a second, near-duplicate index and doubled write cost.

questions.contextHtml:
A jobs table has 120M rows; 99.9% have done = true, a few thousand are done = false. Workers poll SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE done = false ORDER BY created LIMIT 50 every second from 40 workers. Someone added CREATE INDEX ON jobs (done) last quarter. Poll latency is 1.5 s, the index is 4 GB, and the index shows heavy write cost.

-- illustrative
Limit  (actual time=1480..1480 rows=50)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=1480..1480 rows=50)   Sort Method: top-N heapsort
        ->  Index Scan using jobs_done_idx on jobs (actual rows=61342 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (done = false)

Red herring: the team suspects the 40 workers are overloading the connection pool.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index on created too" or "the planner is wrong, force the index". It does not see that a boolean index is huge and mostly useless, nor that a partial index would be tiny.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do rows ever flip back to done=false? How many pending rows at peak? Any other query filtering on done?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Create the partial index below concurrently; polls switch over immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Wrong index shape (dominant, shown by 61k rows read to return 50); lock contention among workers (second); pool (red herring: queries are slow in executor time, not waiting).
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before/after; compare pg_relation_size of old and new index.
  5. Root cause: The index on done contains 120M entries; the planner reads all pending ones, then sorts them by created. The index never helps ordering.
  6. Fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY jobs_pending_idx ON jobs (created) WHERE done = false; Entries exist only for pending rows, so it is KB-sized, ordered, and the LIMIT 50 reads 50 entries. Drop jobs_done_idx. Add FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so workers do not block each other.
  7. Prevention: The query's WHERE clause must imply the index predicate literally (done = false, not a bind parameter that may be generic-planned).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A partial index only serves queries with the same predicate; it also shrinks as rows complete, which keeps it cheap. I would not partition just for this.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY jobs_pending_idx ON jobs (created) WHERE done = false;
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE done = false ORDER BY created LIMIT 50 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if done becomes a status enum with 6 values? -> Partial index per interesting state, or (status, created) with status first if several are polled.
  • Parameterised done = $1? -> The planner may not prove the predicate; use a literal or a separate query.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue table slowed from 2 ms to seconds as history grew; replacing a full index with a partial one dropped it from 6 GB to 80 KB and removed most of the autovacuum churn.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: forces the existing index or adds hardware.
  • Hire: proposes a partial index on the pending rows.
  • Strong hire: ties it to ordering/LIMIT, SKIP LOCKED, parameter pitfalls and concurrent build.

questions.contextHtml: events has 300M rows, 40k tenants, 6 event types, and occurred_at timestamps. The hot query is: SELECT * FROM events WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND occurred_at >= now() - interval '1 day' AND type = $2 ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 100; Existing index: (occurred_at, tenant_id, type). Query takes ~900 ms on a 40-core primary and reads 2M index entries per call.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the index and justify the order. What other query shapes could break your design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Put the most selective column first" without considering that the existing index leads with a range column, or recommends three single-column indexes and hopes for bitmap AND.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do other queries filter by tenant only, or by time only (global reports)? Is type always supplied? Rows per tenant per day?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Build (tenant_id, type, occurred_at DESC) concurrently; keep the old index until the new plan is verified.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Leading range column makes the scan read a full day for every tenant (2M entries); filter by tenant/type happens after the seek.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS): expect Index Cond on all three columns and no Sort, ~100 entries read.
  5. Root cause: Range-first order: only occurred_at narrows the seek; tenant and type are checked per entry.
  6. Fix: Equality columns (tenant_id, type) first, then occurred_at DESC as the sort/range column; LIMIT 100 stops after 100 entries.
  7. Prevention: For each hot query write down E/S/R columns before building the index.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: If type is often omitted, (tenant_id, occurred_at DESC) with type as a filter or INCLUDE column may serve more queries. I would not keep both old and new indexes after migration: the old one costs write amplification on 300M rows.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_tenant_type_time ON events (tenant_id, type, occurred_at DESC);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A global report filters only by time. -> Use a BRIN index on occurred_at if the table is append-only and physically ordered.
  • Tenant skew (one tenant has 40% of rows)? -> The index still works; consider a partial index or partitioning for that tenant if its queries are slow.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Rewriting one composite index from (time, tenant) to (tenant, time) cut p99 from 1.2 s to 6 ms, and write throughput rose 20% after the old index was dropped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: three single-column indexes.
  • Hire: equality first, range last.
  • Strong hire: also handles sort elimination, query-shape trade-offs, BRIN for global time scans and safe migration.

questions.promptHtml: How do InnoDB's clustered index and Postgres's heap-plus-index layout differ, and how does that change your primary key choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reveals whether you know what a secondary index leaf contains and why UUIDs hurt differently.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In InnoDB the primary key B+tree is the table, so rows are stored in PK order and secondary index leaves store the PK value; a secondary lookup is two tree descents. In Postgres the table is an unordered heap and every index leaf stores a TID pointing at the heap, so every lookup is one descent plus one heap jump. Consequently, in InnoDB a wide or random PK hurts the table and every secondary index; in Postgres it mostly hurts the PK index.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
InnoDB:   secondary idx leaf: (email) -> PK value -> PK tree leaf = full row
Postgres: any idx leaf:        (email) -> TID (page, slot) -> heap tuple
  • InnoDB: sequential PKs append to the right edge of the table; random PKs (UUIDv4) split pages across the table and fragment storage. Every secondary index carries a copy of the PK, so a 36-byte string PK balloons them all.
  • Postgres: heap tuple placement is independent of the PK; a random UUID only makes the PK B-tree insertions random. Updates create new tuple versions and new TIDs, so indexes need new entries unless HOT applies.
  • Covering: InnoDB secondary index (a) already covers (a, pk) queries.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Carrying InnoDB advice ("always use auto-increment") to Postgres unchanged.
  • Choosing UUIDv4 as clustered PK on a table larger than RAM.
  • Assuming a Postgres PK means the table is physically ordered (it is not; CLUSTER is a one-time sort).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What should I use instead of UUIDv4? -> Time-ordered ids (UUIDv7, ULID, bigint) so inserts hit the rightmost leaf.
  2. Why is a secondary lookup in InnoDB costlier? -> Two descents; mitigated by covering the query in the secondary index.
  3. Postgres updates and indexes? -> Each non-HOT update adds an entry to every index since the TID changes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "InnoDB clusters". Senior: effect on secondary-index size, insert locality, cache behaviour and HOT updates, with a PK recommendation per engine.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A MySQL table with a CHAR(36) PK made every secondary index 4x larger, and buffer pool hit ratio fell until ids were switched to a time-ordered bigint.

questions.subtopic: Index-only scan that still hits the heap
questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service runs SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = $1 at 6,000 req/s. Last sprint you added CREATE INDEX wallets_user_inc ON wallets (user_id) INCLUDE (balance) to get an index-only scan. Load tests looked great; in production p99 is 40 ms and disk read IOPS are 3x higher than expected. The table is updated ~2,000 times/s (balance changes).

-- illustrative
Index Only Scan using wallets_user_inc on wallets (actual time=0.02..0.31 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (user_id = 8123)
  Heap Fetches: 1
  Buffers: shared hit=3 read=1

Red herring: someone points at shared_buffers being too small.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the "index-only" scan still reading the heap and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase shared_buffers" or "the index is not covering", missing the visibility map and that the INCLUDE column itself is the hot-updated column.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often is each row updated? Autovacuum settings on this table? Do reads need the freshest balance (yes, so no stale cache)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing destructive; check Heap Fetches across a sample and the VM bits: SELECT relallvisible, relpages FROM pg_class WHERE relname='wallets';.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) visibility map bits cleared by constant updates, so each page needs a heap visit; (b) the covering column is updated, so no HOT updates and the index churns; (c) autovacuum too slow; (d) shared_buffers (low, hit=3 suggests cache is fine).
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows Heap Fetches near the row count; pg_stat_user_tables for n_tup_hot_upd vs n_tup_upd; pg_stat_user_indexes for index size growth.
  5. Root cause: Index-only scans only skip the heap on pages marked all-visible. On a table updated thousands of times per second, pages are almost never all-visible. Worse, indexing balance forces every update to write a new index entry (no HOT).
  6. Fix: Drop the INCLUDE of the hot column: keep (user_id) only; the heap page is almost surely cached and a point lookup costs one extra hit. Lower autovacuum scale factor for this table if you still want index-only on other queries.
  7. Prevention: Only add covering columns that are rarely updated; load-test with realistic write rates; alert on Heap Fetches / rows for key queries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add more INCLUDE columns, nor crank autovacuum to run constantly; a covering index on a hot-update column loses on both read and write sides.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would a fillfactor help? -> Lower table fillfactor (e.g. 80) leaves room for HOT updates when no indexed column changes.
  • And for a read-mostly table? -> Then covering works great once vacuum has set the VM bits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "balance" INCLUDE doubled WAL volume and index size; removing it reduced WAL by 35% and p99 by half, despite looking like a pure read optimisation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes shared_buffers.
  • Hire: knows Index Only Scan needs the visibility map.
  • Strong hire: connects HOT updates, covering-column churn and autovacuum, with a measured decision.

questions.promptHtml: What is a HOT update in Postgres, and how do indexes and INCLUDE columns affect it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat index additions as a read-only decision from those who know the write path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Postgres never updates a row in place; it writes a new tuple version. Normally every index needs a new entry pointing at the new TID. A HOT (heap-only tuple) update skips index maintenance when no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same heap page. Indexing or INCLUDE-ing a frequently updated column disables HOT for those updates, so write cost, WAL and bloat rise.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
non-HOT:  heap: old v1 -> new v2 (new page maybe)  + new entry in EVERY index
HOT:      heap: v1 -> v2 same page, chained via line pointer; indexes untouched
  • Requirements: no indexed column (including INCLUDE and expression/partial predicate columns) changed; free space on the page (fillfactor < 100 helps).
  • Dead HOT chains are pruned on page access without a full VACUUM, so HOT also reduces vacuum load.
  • Monitoring: n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables.
  • Covering indexes: INCLUDE only stores payload in leaves, but any change to that value forces a new index tuple, so no HOT.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT relname, n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd,
       round(100.0*n_tup_hot_upd/nullif(n_tup_upd,0),1) AS hot_pct
FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_tup_upd DESC LIMIT 10;
ALTER TABLE wallets SET (fillfactor = 85);  -- room on page for HOT; applies to new pages / after rewrite

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Indexing updated_at or a counter "for sorting".
  • Thinking fillfactor affects existing pages immediately (it needs a rewrite or new pages).
  • Assuming InnoDB behaves the same (it updates in place and uses undo).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does HOT reduce VACUUM work? -> Chains are pruned during normal page access and no index entries become dead.
  2. What breaks HOT besides indexes? -> A full page: the new version must fit on the same page.
  3. Can you check which index breaks HOT? -> Compare the updated columns with pg_index definitions; drop or move the churny column out of the index.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "indexes slow writes". Senior: names HOT, its conditions, the metric to watch and the fillfactor lever, and applies it to an INCLUDE decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A counters table with an index on the counter column had 0% HOT updates and 12x bloat; moving the counter off the indexed set and lowering fillfactor stabilised it.

questions.subtopic: Building indexes on a live table
questions.contextHtml:
You must add (tenant_id, status) to invoices (600M rows, 200 GB) on the primary of a payments system doing 3,000 writes/s. The first attempt, run by a teammate with plain CREATE INDEX, queued writes for 8 minutes and caused API 500s when the connection pool filled. Second attempt with CONCURRENTLY failed after 2 hours with ERROR: deadlock detected during the second scan. Now pg_index shows:

-- illustrative
 indexrelid          | indisvalid | indisready
 invoices_tenant_idx | f          | t

A replica is also used for reporting. Disk headroom is 90 GB.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just rerun it" without cleaning up the invalid index, or "take downtime", or ignoring disk, replicas and the long-transaction interaction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What else was running (long transactions, other DDL)? Is there a maintenance window? What are the lock timeouts? Is the replica lagging?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Writes are fine now; the invalid index still costs maintenance on every write, so decide fast: drop it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) concurrent DDL or a long transaction interfered (CONCURRENTLY waits for old snapshots and can deadlock with other DDL); (b) the invalid index is a leftover from the failed build; (c) disk pressure from temp sort files.
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid; pg_stat_activity for old xact_start; pg_stat_progress_create_index during the build; df on tablespace.
  5. Root cause: A concurrent build does two table scans and waits for all transactions that predate each phase; a long transaction or other DDL stalls or deadlocks it, leaving an INVALID index that still receives writes.
  6. Fix: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY invoices_tenant_idx; Then terminate or wait out long transactions, set lock_timeout = '5s', maintenance_work_mem to a few GB, and re-run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Estimate 2x index size of temp space (~10 to 30 GB) against 90 GB headroom; watch replica lag.
  7. Prevention: Run index builds in a runbook with pre-checks (no long transactions, no other DDL); migration tooling that checks for NOT indisvalid; alert on invalid indexes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not take downtime, and I would not leave the invalid index in place (it is used for nothing and costs writes). A concurrent build takes longer and uses more I/O, which I accept for no write block.
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
SET maintenance_work_mem = '4GB';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY invoices_tenant_status_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, status);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can I run it inside a transaction block? -> No; CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction.
  • Replica reports slow during the build? -> WAL replay of the build competes; throttle with maintenance I/O settings or build off-peak.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A forgotten idle in transaction session from a notebook held the snapshot for 3 days; every concurrent build waited behind it until we killed the session and added a timeout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reruns blindly or takes downtime.
  • Hire: drops the invalid index, uses CONCURRENTLY, checks long transactions.
  • Strong hire: sizes disk, sets lock_timeout and maintenance_work_mem, watches progress and replicas, and prevents recurrence.

questions.subtopic: How the planner picks index vs seq scan
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how Postgres decides between a sequential scan, an index scan and a bitmap scan for a filter, and which knobs shift that decision.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes whether you can reason about "why wasn't my index used" from cost, not folklore.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The planner estimates the fraction of rows the filter keeps from statistics, then costs each path. A seq scan reads all pages sequentially (cheap per page, seq_page_cost 1.0). An index scan does random heap reads (random_page_cost, 4.0 by default), so it wins only for a small fraction. A bitmap scan sits between: it sorts matching page numbers and reads each heap page once. Raising the matched fraction, or lowering the random cost, moves the crossover.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Illustrative costs for 10M rows, 80k pages: seq ~ 80,000x1.0 + 10M x 0.01 = 180,000. Index for 1,000 matches ~ 1,000 x 4.0 plus index pages = ~4,500, index wins ~40x. At 3M matches, an index plan costs ~12M and seq wins.

rows kept:  tiny ----------- medium ------------- large
plan:       Index Scan      Bitmap Heap Scan      Seq Scan
  • ORDER BY ... LIMIT flips the rule: an index in sort order can stop after N rows even when many rows match.
  • Correlation (pg_stats.correlation) matters: a column physically ordered with the heap makes index scans cheaper.
  • random_page_cost around 1.1 on SSD pushes toward indexes; effective_cache_size also affects index cost.
  • Wrong estimates, not the rule of thumb, are the usual reason for a surprise: stale stats, correlated predicates, generic prepared plans.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off;   -- diagnosis only: does an index plan exist, and is it actually faster?
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating "index scan good, seq scan bad" as a rule.
  • Leaving random_page_cost at 4.0 on NVMe and forcing indexes with hints.
  • Using enable_seqscan = off in production instead of diagnosis.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would a 20% filter use a bitmap scan? -> It coalesces random reads into page-ordered ones, cheaper than plain index scan and cheaper than reading all pages when matches are concentrated.
  2. Why can a LIMIT 10 use the index on a 60% filter? -> Early termination: the cost is proportional to rows needed, not matched.
  3. How do you verify the planner's belief? -> Compare rows= with actual rows=, then check pg_stats for that column.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "index if selective, otherwise seq scan". Senior: cost model, bitmap middle ground, LIMIT effect, correlation, SSD tuning and where estimate errors come from.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving to NVMe with the default random_page_cost left plans choosing seq scans on 5% filters until the setting was lowered and verified.

questions.contextHtml:
An ingestion table readings has 14 indexes and sustains 2,000 inserts/s. Product wants 20,000/s next quarter. CPU is 40%, but iowait and WAL volume are high: WAL grows at ~160 MB/s; replica lag spikes to minutes. pg_stat_user_indexes on the primary (stats reset 9 days ago):

-- illustrative
indexrelname           idx_scan  size
readings_dev_ts          5.1M    18 GB
readings_dev            12.0M     9 GB
readings_ts                 0    14 GB
readings_dev_ts_val        40    22 GB
readings_flag               0     3 GB
...(9 more, mixed)

A BI team uses a replica for month-end reports.
questions.promptHtml: How do you prune indexes safely and what is the plan for 10x writes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Drop every index with idx_scan = 0 on the primary" with no thought for replicas, month-end jobs, stats resets or constraint indexes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When were stats reset and what is the longest query cycle (month-end, quarterly)? Which indexes back constraints/FKs? Is the BI replica its own stats domain?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce replica lag by batching inserts (COPY, 1k to 10k rows per transaction); no drops yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) each insert updates 14 B-trees and WALs all of them; (b) overlapping indexes: (dev) is a prefix of (dev, ts); (c) wide index readings_dev_ts_val with INCLUDE-ish bloat; (d) full_page_writes after checkpoints inflating WAL.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_user_indexes on every replica, pg_stat_statements for query shapes, pg_constraint/pg_index for uniqueness and FK use, WAL rate from pg_stat_wal.
  5. Root cause: Write amplification: 14 index inserts per row, many redundant. Insert cost scales with index count and random leaf touches.
  6. Fix: Drop readings_dev (covered by (dev, ts)), readings_ts and readings_flag after confirming no month-end use; rename-then-wait is not possible for indexes, so take a pg_get_indexdef backup to recreate. Replace big BTREE on ts with BRIN if table is append-ordered. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  7. Prevention: Index review in code review with a query evidence requirement; quarterly audit; dashboard of write amplification (WAL bytes per row).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop an index only seen unused on one node. For 10x, I would also consider time-partitioning so recent partitions have small hot indexes, and keep older ones read-only.
SELECT s.indexrelname, s.idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) size,
       i.indisunique OR i.indisprimary AS backs_constraint
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s JOIN pg_index i USING (indexrelid)
WHERE s.relname = 'readings' ORDER BY s.idx_scan;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Stats were reset yesterday on the replica? -> Wait for a full business cycle or review query logs; idx_scan resets with the stats.
  • Throughput still short after pruning? -> Partition by time, batch writes, synchronous_commit tradeoffs only if the data tolerates it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Pruning 5 of 12 indexes took ingest from 3k to 11k rows/s; a month later a quarterly report found the one we dropped, which we rebuilt off-peak, hence the "keep a definition backup" step.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: drops by idx_scan on one node.
  • Hire: checks replicas and prefix overlap.
  • Strong hire: adds constraint checks, cycle windows, BRIN/partitioning and batching for 10x.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A session store table sessions (40M rows, deletes and inserts constantly, TTL purge nightly) saw lookups by token degrade from 0.2 ms to 25 ms over 3 months; no alerts fired. The index sessions_token_idx was 30 GB where the live data needed ~8 GB. During the incident someone ran REINDEX INDEX sessions_token_idx in business hours; writes blocked for 4 minutes, the API errored, and the incident widened.

-- illustrative (pgstattuple-style)
index_size: 31 GB   avg_leaf_density: 24%   leaf_fragmentation: 61%
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident discussion: what failed, what do you fix now and what do you change so it does not recur?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run VACUUM FULL" (locks the table), or "reindex more often" with no monitoring and no explanation of why bloat formed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is autovacuum doing on this table? Any long transactions pinning the horizon? Which Postgres version (REINDEX CONCURRENTLY is 12+)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY sessions_token_idx; off-peak; plain REINDEX takes a lock that blocks writes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) churn plus a purge deleting millions of rows at once leaves sparse leaves that B-tree reuse cannot fully recover; (b) autovacuum lagging; (c) a long transaction blocking cleanup; (d) a random token key causing scattered fragmentation.
  4. How I'd verify: pgstatindex() from pgstattuple (avg_leaf_density), pg_stat_user_tables (n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum), oldest xact_start.
  5. Root cause: No size or density monitoring, a bulk nightly delete, and a reflex that used a blocking command in peak hours.
  6. Fix: Short term: concurrent reindex. Long term: partition sessions by day and drop old partitions (no delete churn, no bloat), or purge in small batches; tune autovacuum for this table.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on index size vs expected, pgstatindex density check weekly, runbook that forbids non-concurrent DDL on hot tables, lock_timeout on migrations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Partitioning adds query and maintenance complexity; I accept it for TTL tables. I would not use VACUUM FULL (exclusive lock, rewrites the table) and not rely on pg_repack blindly without testing on a copy.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT avg_leaf_density, leaf_fragmentation FROM pgstatindex('sessions_token_idx');
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY sessions_token_idx;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• REINDEX CONCURRENTLY failed midway? -> It leaves an invalid _ccnew index; drop it and retry.
  • Why not just lower autovacuum thresholds? -> Helps, but bulk deletes still create sparse pages; partition drop is cleaner.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A TTL table moved to daily partitions; the nightly purge became a DROP TABLE in milliseconds and index size stayed flat for a year.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the database or reruns blocking commands.
  • Hire: concurrent reindex and bloat explanation.
  • Strong hire: root causes in design (bulk deletes, no monitoring), partitioning and process fixes.

questions.contextHtml:
Product asks: "Make the customer search box fast." The backend runs SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%' OR email ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%' LIMIT 20 on 25M rows. It takes 6 s. A colleague proposes CREATE INDEX ON customers (name) and (email); they tested it on 10k rows and it was "instant".

-- illustrative
Seq Scan on customers (actual time=0.1..5900 rows=20 loops=1)
  Filter: ((name ~~* '%ann%') OR (email ~~* '%ann%'))
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add B-tree indexes on both columns" (leading wildcard cannot use them) or "move to Elasticsearch" without asking about requirements.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it prefix, substring or typo-tolerant search? Minimum characters typed? Expected QPS? Must results be ranked? Acceptable staleness?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Require 3+ characters and cap results; add a statement_timeout so the query cannot hog CPU.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Leading wildcard defeats B-tree order; OR across two columns blocks a single index; tiny test data hid it.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-sized data (or a restored copy); check pg_trgm availability.
  5. Root cause: A B-tree is sorted by prefix; %ann% has no usable range, so the planner must test every row.
  6. Fix: pg_trgm with GIN: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON customers USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops), (email gin_trgm_ops). The planner can BitmapOr the two indexes. For prefix-only needs, use text_pattern_ops B-tree with LIKE 'ann%'. For ranked or fuzzy search at scale, a search engine or Postgres full-text search.
  7. Prevention: Test with production-scale data; keep a "slow query on prod copy" check in CI for search endpoints.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Trigram GIN indexes are large (often comparable to the data) and slow writes; fine for a search table, costly on hot tables. I would not bolt on a new search system before confirming the requirement.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cust_name_trgm ON customers USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cust_email_trgm ON customers USING gin (email gin_trgm_ops);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users type 1 or 2 characters? -> Trigrams barely filter; enforce a minimum length or prefix search.
  • Need typo tolerance and ranking? -> similarity() with trigram, or a dedicated engine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A search feature passed QA on a 5k-row staging DB and brought production to 100% CPU on launch day; a trigram index plus a 3-character minimum fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes B-tree indexes.
  • Hire: identifies leading wildcard and suggests pg_trgm.
  • Strong hire: starts with requirements, picks the proportionate tool, notes index size and write cost.
